# The Pleasures of Being Lost

A map is an argument about what matters. It shows the roads, railways, rivers, and boundaries that someone decided were important enough to record. It names a hospital but may omit the bakery where you bought breakfast. It marks a park as a clean green shape while leaving out the bench where someone once sat and watched rain darken the sky. A map is useful precisely because it leaves things out; otherwise it would be as large and complicated as the world itself. Yet we sometimes forget that every map is a selective account, a way of arranging reality according to a purpose. The map used by a driver, a walker, a bird, or a person looking for a quiet place may describe entirely different territories. And beyond the edges of all of them lies the territory of getting lost.

There is a particular pleasure in discovering that you have misunderstood where you are. It arrives first as a small uncertainty, then as a glance down at the map, then as a second glance at the street sign whose name you are suddenly no longer certain you have read correctly. For a moment, the planned route becomes only one possibility among many. The destination does not disappear, exactly, but it loosens its grip on the imagination. You begin to notice things that would have been invisible if you had known precisely where you were going: an alley filled with bicycles, a wall covered in flowering vines, the sound of metal shutters being pulled across a shopfront, a cat observing you from a windowsill with professional calm.

I once got lost in a city I had never visited, following a paper map in the age before phones offered to guide us. I turned down a street because it looked interesting, then took another turn, then discovered that the neat lines on the map no longer matched anything I could see. The error felt more consequential than it would have at home. I was a stranger among strangers, and the names around me seemed to belong to a private language. A woman carrying a basket of apples directed me toward a church, but the church was apparently not the church I needed. A boy pointed in the opposite direction and then, after reconsidering, pointed back the way I had come. I laughed, and he laughed too, and for a few minutes we were collaborators in a project neither of us had planned.

Eventually I found the correct street. The journey had taken forty minutes longer than it should have. If I had followed the fastest route, I would have arrived on time and remembered almost nothing. Instead, I remember a narrow passage with a blue door, the smell of oranges being peeled in a market, and a small square where three streets met beneath plane trees. Years have thinned the memory, but it has not erased it. The wrong turn became a room I could still enter. This is one of the gentle paradoxes of getting lost: it sometimes gives us more vivid memories than success would have.

Paper maps have a quality that digital navigation cannot quite reproduce. They are objects, fragile and folded, requiring a relationship of trust. You have to turn them around, calculate which direction you are facing, and forgive their limited accuracy. The marks are not moving. The blue dot that announces your position is not following you down the street, updating itself, insisting that you are here. Instead, you must locate yourself through reasoning, observation, and a willingness to be briefly mistaken. The map does not eliminate uncertainty; it gives uncertainty a surface on which to work.

There is something almost charming about this. We live amid an abundance of information, yet the most ordinary actions have become surprisingly difficult to perform without assistance. We ask devices to tell us which way to walk, which store is open, whether the traffic is bad, where the nearest charging point is, what the weather will do by lunchtime. A generation ago, these questions were answered by memory, habit, or the ability to read the landscape. We did not think of that knowledge as remarkable because it was embedded in daily life. We knew which turn led to the bus stop, which door was usually propped open, which corner smelled different after rain. We possessed a private geography made from thousands of small discoveries.

Maps also teach us to distrust certain kinds of experience. A person might tell us that the museum is “just ahead,” but the map says that it should still be three streets away. A path may look shortest on paper while climbing a steep hill in reality. A bridge may be drawn as a solid line even when it is closed for repairs. A road may exist in the mapmaker’s knowledge but not in the lived world. The map tells us what should be there; the walk tells us what is there. Both are true, but they are not speaking the same language.

The difference is easiest to understand through memory. We rarely remember a journey by its official distances. We remember where we had to stop and ask for directions. We remember the unexpected thunderstorm, the restaurant where we waited out the rain, the view from a side road. A successful journey can be almost weightless afterward. Nobody writes a poem because they took the correct turn. The detour has texture. It has resistance. It demands that we participate.

This is why children seem to understand maps more instinctively than adults do. A child given a map does not necessarily see it as a set of instructions. For a child, it may resemble a picture, a puzzle, or an invitation to imagine what lies beyond the visible lines. Children are not yet fully enslaved by efficiency. They may stop to examine a storm drain because it looks like a small metal face. They may draw imaginary roads across the map, connecting a castle to a submarine, a bakery to a planet. Their maps are inaccurate, but they are not necessarily poor. They are playful. They turn the world into a place that can be reinterpreted.

As adults, we become increasingly suspicious of anything that cannot be immediately justified. We want the optimal route, the efficient system, the neatly summarized conclusion. We compress decisions into menus and turn experiences into ratings. We ask whether a place is worth visiting before we have actually seen it, whether a book is difficult, whether a conversation is going well enough to continue. The destination becomes more important than the journey not because we are necessarily bad people, but because the world rewards those who can move through it quickly. Yet speed has a way of becoming a philosophy, and a philosophy can quietly become a cage.

The arrival of digital maps changed getting lost in both obvious and less obvious ways. On one hand, they have made travel safer and more accessible. Someone who does not speak the local language can still find a station or a hospital. A driver can navigate unfamiliar roads without having to study a folded sheet of paper. A lost child can be located more quickly. A person with a disability may find routes that would once have seemed impossible. These are genuine improvements, and it would be foolish to romanticize the inconvenience of not knowing where you are.

On the other hand, digital navigation has changed the texture of attention. A traditional map requires us to look outward. A phone often allows us to look down. We walk through a city while seeing a small glass rectangle that tells us what to do next. The route is no longer something we interpret; it is something delivered to us. The blue dot is reassuring, but it can also become a tiny theater of anxiety. When the dot moves inaccurately, when the voice gives an abrupt instruction, when the estimated arrival time increases by four minutes, we experience a minor rupture in our sense of control.

The screen does not simply show us the city. It competes with it. One eye is on the street, the other is on the route. A tree, a fountain, a beautiful doorway, a face across the street: all are available to be noticed, but the phone creates a structure in which noticing must occur alongside management. This is why a wrong turn can feel so irritating when we are following a device. The device has promised that confusion will be removed, so any uncertainty feels like a failure of the promise. We are not only lost in the city; we are lost in our expectation that we should never be lost at all.

There are places where I still distrust the blue dot. In an old neighborhood with winding lanes, the signal fades behind thick walls. A street shown on the screen turns out to be a pedestrian passage. A shop marked on the map has moved, closed, or become something else. The map becomes less like a reliable guide and more like a historical document, evidence of a city that existed according to its creators’ plans. I sometimes turn the phone away and navigate by the sun, by the slope of the ground, by the direction of traffic. This does not always work. But the uncertainty restores a relationship with place that the screen had temporarily dissolved.

The best journeys are not necessarily the ones with the most dramatic events. Sometimes they are the ones that leave room for the unplanned. A traveler who spends three hours in a town because the bus was delayed may discover the rhythm of its mornings: the delivery carts, the shutters opening, the old men who sit outside the café, the schoolchildren crossing at the same corner every day. Without the delay, there would be no such knowledge. The traveler would have passed through, seen the listed attraction, taken a photograph, and left. The place would have remained a destination rather than becoming an experience.

The same principle applies to conversations. A person may begin by asking what they do for work and end up telling you about a fear they have never spoken aloud. A discussion about a book may drift into a memory of childhood. An argument may reveal a disagreement beneath the apparent disagreement. These moments are not always pleasant. They are not always welcome. But they occur because the conversation has escaped the narrow route both people had planned for it. The destination—agreement, certainty, a clear answer—matters less than the willingness to remain in the room a little longer than expected.

We speak casually about being lost in thought, in love, in music, in time, and in the past. These expressions suggest that getting lost is not only a problem of physical navigation. It is a condition that can happen to the mind. We lose ourselves in a book because its pages have created a temporary country with its own customs and dangers. We lose ourselves in music because a melody has opened a door we did not know was there. We lose ourselves in love because another person has become a landscape we must learn to inhabit. We lose ourselves in memory because the past sometimes returns with greater emotional clarity than the present.

Perhaps this is why getting lost can feel both frightening and attractive. The known world is comfortable, but it can also become too small. Familiar rooms begin to repeat themselves. Routine protects us, but it can also narrow the range of what we are able to notice. A little uncertainty shakes the walls loose. It makes us look again. It forces us to ask questions we would otherwise avoid: What else is nearby? What have I been ignoring? What would happen if I took the other road?

The answer cannot be that everyone should abandon plans, maps, or schedules. Most responsibilities require direction. Someone must know where the child is. Someone must know when the train leaves. Someone must know how to find the fire exit in an unfamiliar building. The point is not to celebrate ignorance indiscriminately, but to remember that usefulness and fullness are not identical. A life organized entirely around efficiency may be safe, productive, and strangely uninhabited. The unplanned portions are where much of the meaning accumulates.

There is also a difference between getting lost and being excluded. To romanticize every form of disorientation can be insulting to people whose maps have been drawn for them, whose routes have been closed, whose neighborhoods are policed, whose movement through the world is monitored or restricted. Many people do not experience uncertainty as a gift. For them, being lost may mean missing a connection, losing documents, facing harassment, or being stranded somewhere hostile. The privilege of getting lost depends on having enough security to recover from it. Freedom to wander is not evenly distributed.

Even in ordinary life, a wrong turn is more serious when it occurs at night, in a dangerous neighborhood, or while carrying a small child. A person who is lost in a familiar park at noon may find the adventure charming. A person who is lost in a city after a flight delay may be frightened. The romantic language of wandering should not erase these differences. The point is not that confusion is always good. It is that a culture needs room for uncertainty, and that room can be created without pretending all uncertainty is harmless.

Cities themselves are full of unofficial maps. Children know the routes that are too narrow for cars. Shopkeepers know which alley is safest after closing time. Bus drivers know where passengers usually gather when the official stop has been moved. Tour guides know which stories make strangers listen. Residents know which trees mark a hidden staircase, which windows belong to families that leave a radio playing, which corner catches the sun in winter. These maps are made from repeated attention. They are not printed, sold, or updated by software companies. They are passed between people, often in the form of casual conversation: “Go past the blue door. Turn where the old woman hangs the laundry. You’ll see it.”

The most important places in a life are not always the ones with the most precise coordinates. A friend’s kitchen is located through a sequence of sensations: the squeak of the gate, the particular sound of the kettle, the dog that barks only at delivery drivers. A childhood garden is remembered by the smell of cut grass and the location of a low brick wall. A favorite bench may matter less for its view than for the conversations held there. We do not navigate these places by distance alone. We navigate them by memory, emotion, and the traces other people have left behind.

This is why returning to a familiar place after a long absence can feel like getting lost. The place remains, but we have changed. We notice alterations that once would have been invisible. A shop is missing. A street looks narrower. A tree has grown over a wall. The old route no longer corresponds to the person we have become. Home can be a place of profound recognition and strange displacement at the same time. We may ask ourselves where we belong, or whether belonging is something that must be rebuilt rather than rediscovered.

The language of travel encourages us to think of a destination as the point that gives a journey meaning. We save for it, plan around it, measure our progress toward it. But many of the strongest memories I have are not of destinations. They are of pauses: a station platform in the early morning, a road after a summer storm, a hotel room where the curtains prevented the streetlight from entering, a kitchen table after everyone else had gone to sleep. These moments are not empty intervals between important events. They are the events themselves.

Perhaps the most useful way to think about getting lost is as a correction. It corrects the assumption that attention is automatic. It corrects the belief that knowledge is equivalent to control. It corrects the habit of treating every experience as something to be optimized. To get lost is to discover that the world contains more than the route you had in mind. It is a reminder that the map, however good, is never the whole country.

We do not need to make a grand gesture to recover this feeling. We can take a walk without plotting every turn. We can put the phone in a pocket and allow ourselves to be temporarily uncertain. We can visit a neighborhood by choosing a street rather than searching for an address. We can leave a little space in the day for the unplanned. We can ask someone how they are and resist the urge to redirect the conversation toward an efficient conclusion. We can let a book be difficult, a silence be long, a friendship be unseasonably complicated.

The goal is not to be lost forever. It is to return with more awareness than we had before. A destination is useful, but it should not be allowed to become a reason to fail to see the road. The next time the street does not match the plan, the next time the instructions are insufficient, the next time a familiar world opens into a country of surprises, it may be worth asking not only, “How do I get back?” but also, “What is here that I did not expect to find?”
